transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-20 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~60 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Theo Alvarez (Redwood CSM); Carlos Rivera, Priya Nair, Liam O'Connor, Dana Wu (Nebula)

Summary: 60-minute scoping to align on benchmark harness integration, workload profiles (burst vs steady), streaming vs non-streaming tradeoffs, success criteria (latency p95/p99, cost per 1M tokens, error budget), and timeline for POC runs. Action items captured at end.

Topics: harness onboarding, trace collection, traffic ramp strategy, streaming vs non-streaming, autoscaling/queueing behaviour, security/compliance handoffs.

---- Transcript ----
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everybody, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:03] Carlos: Carlos here.
[00:05] Priya: Priya here.
[00:06] Liam: Liam, yep.
[00:08] Dana: Dana here.
[00:10] Jordan: Great. I'll hand off to Maya to give a quick runbook for the harness then we dig into your workload.
[00:16] Maya: Cool, thanks. So the Redwood benchmark harness is basically a dockerized runner that can replay traces or run synthetic generators. We have two modes—recorded-trace replay and synthetic load. The harness supports streaming (chunked responses) and non-streaming (call-and-wait) patterns. There's an example harness-config.yaml in the repo.
[00:34] Priya: Quick question — what's the difference operationally, I mean what should we expect to change between streaming and non-streaming?
[00:39] Maya: Good question. Streaming preserves lower first-byte latency for long-running generations, but it does change CPU/GPU scheduling because you have many in-flight partial responses. Non-streaming can be more batch-friendly and sometimes achieves better GPU utilization for high throughput, but first-token latency increases — so if your product needs immediate partial results streaming is better.
[01:02] Carlos: Our main use case is regenerative note drafting where a clinician sees partial text as it's generated. So streaming is preferred from UX POV, but our SRE worries about tail latencies and cost.
[01:12] Liam: Right — we care about p95 and p99 both, and our SLA is 500ms p95 for short prompts (<128 tokens). For longer prompts and >1024 tokens we have softer SLOs.
[01:24] Maya: Ok that helps. For the harness we'll simulate both short interactive flows and long batched generations. We typically recommend a 70/30 split streaming/non-streaming in the first pass if UX requires it.
[01:34] Theo: Also note we'll instrument KV cache warm paths — some transcripts mention 'key value cash' in past notes because of transcriber typos — but it's the KV cache hit rate that changes latency dramatically.
[01:42] Priya: We do use a prefix cache in prod — our hit rate is usually 45% during business hours. Is that enough to change the test profile?
[01:49] Maya: Yes, absolutely. We'll parameterize the harness to replay traces with the same hit-rate distribution. If you can provide sampled request logs and KV cache indicators, we can mirror that.
[01:59] Jordan: Can you remind everyone what success looks like for Nebula? Carlos?
[02:03] Carlos: Two things — first, we need latency under SLOs for 95% of requests and predictable cost per 1M tokens estimated; second, validate that dedicated vs hosted modes hit throughput targets with our expected concurrency. If hosted fails we need a path to Redwood Dedicated or private deploy.
[02:19] Maya: Great; we'll include a table of p50/p95/p99 and cost per million tokens in the benchmark report.
[02:26] Priya: On the traces — we can scrub PHI but want to keep distributional properties. We'll aim to provide 72h traces.
[02:33] Jordan: Perfect. Let's dig into workload sizing. Priya, what's your current peak QPS and concurrency?
[02:38] Priya: Peak steady QPS is about 120 req/s for short prompts during clinics, spikes up to ~450 req/s during morning sync window for batch jobs. Average token output per request is 220, short prompts ~40 tokens.
[02:51] Maya: So for benchmark we should model at least three buckets: interactive short (<128 tokens) 60% of traffic, medium (128-512) 30%, long (>512) 10%. Also run a spike test to 2x expected peak to validate autoscale.
[03:08] Liam: For spike tests we need to observe tail behavior; we can't have long queuing that pushes p99 to multiple seconds.
[03:13] Maya: Agreed — harness will measure queue time, GPU schedule time, first-token latency. We'll surface p50/p90/p95/p99 and also measured token/sec per GPU.
[03:23] Carlos: What about batching? If we enable dynamic batching will we get better throughput for non-streaming loads?
[03:29] Maya: Yes, dynamic batching helps a lot for non-streaming long sequences, but it increases latency for individual requests unless you set tight batching windows. For streaming, batching is harder because partial responses break up batchable windows. We can test with batching window sizes 5ms/10ms/20ms to see cost/latency tradeoffs.
[03:44] Priya: Do you support mixed routing — e.g., route interactive to low-latency pool and long batch jobs to a high-throughput cost-optimized pool?
[03:51] Jordan: Yes that's one of the smart-routing options. We'll propose a policy you can pin in the POC: interactive->low-latency hosted variant, batch->quantized model variant or dedicated node pool.
[03:59] [05:00] Speaker 1: Sorry random mic issue —
[05:01] Maya: No worries. Back to metrics: we should define test matrix. I'll read it out: recorded-trace replay (3 x 10-minute windows: steady, morning spike, low-traffic), synthetic ramp (linear ramp 0->2xpeak over 15 minutes), soak (30 min at peak), spike bursts (10s high-QPS bursts). For each mode run streaming and non-streaming variants.
[05:31] Priya: That looks good. For soak do you mean sustained at our current peak (120) or the 450 spike?
[05:37] Maya: Soak at nominal peak 120, and a separate soak at the 450 cluster for a shorter period. We'll annotate each with concurrency targets.
[05:45] Carlos: What's the expected run time for the full matrix?
[05:48] Maya: Full matrix with all permutations might be 6-8 hours. We'll run the minimal matrix for POC (about 2 hours) focusing on most critical flows and then schedule extended runs if needed.
[05:59] Liam: Important to note — our infra has a 30-second cold-start penalty for some on-demand instances, which skews p99. Can you simulate node cold starts?
[06:08] Maya: We can parameterize cold-start occurrences; we typically inject 1% cold starts in the trace to model this behaviour.
[06:15] Dana: On compliance, will the harness or logs include any data that could be PHI? We need to validate redaction.
[06:21] Jordan: We'll not transfer raw PHI. Priya will upload sanitized traces. For toolchains we support client-side tokenization or KMS integrations for private deploy.
[06:29] Dana: Good. Also provide SOC2 docs and a list of data paths for the audit.
[06:33] Jordan: Noted, Theo will follow up.
[06:35] Theo: I'll share SOC2 + Syslog mapping by EOD.
[06:38] Maya: Back to scripting specifics — the harness has a script/adapter for your auth flow and header signing. Priya, do you use a custom JWT or standard OIDC?
[06:46] Priya: OIDC via our internal IdP but we have a token-exchange step.
[06:50] Maya: Ok we'll add a small adapter so the harness can mint test tokens. We'll keep it in a sandbox and not touch production IdP.
[06:57] Carlos: For the canonical prompt set, we want 200 prompts representative across specialties. We'll pick 50 each from cardiology, oncology, general practice, and admin templates.
[07:06] Jordan: Perfect. That will help measure semantic quality too, but for this engagement the primary success metrics are latency and cost. We'll also run a small eval to detect quality regressions after we test quantized variants.
[07:16] Priya: Regarding quantized models — we need to know expected degradation and likely savings. Can you provide a delta table?
[07:22] Maya: We'll include model variants in the report: fp16 baseline, 4-bit quantized (LLM-Q4) and int8 where supported. Expect 2-3x compute cost reduction for heavy sequences with minor quality delta for many tasks but we'll validate on your prompts.
[07:36] Liam: About metrics collection — what tracing format do you ingest? Jaeger, OpenTelemetry?
[07:41] Maya: We emit OpenTelemetry traces and a CSV summary with token counts and latencies. The harness can push to your S3 or a shared bucket.
[07:48] Priya: Nice. Can we get raw per-request CSV so our internal analysis team can re-run?
[07:52] Maya: Yes we'll provide raw CSVs and a condensed report with aggregated percentiles.
[07:56] [08:00] Speaker 2: small crosstalk, hold on —
[08:05] Carlos: Let's talk about cost modeling. For our budgeting we need an estimate per 1M tokens at p95 SLO. How do you derive that?
[08:12] Jordan: Our report will include cost breakdown by GPU time, networking, and any call overheads. We'll surface tokens/generated vs compute-seconds and convert to an expected cost per 1M tokens under each model variant and batching window.
[08:25] Priya: And include license/reserved cost if Dedicated is chosen?
[08:28] Jordan: Yes, we'll include a reserved vs on-demand comparison and amortized monthly cost.
[08:33] Maya: For benchmarking we'll estimate token/sec/GPU and multiply by effective utilization given your batch windows and cache hit rate.
[08:41] Liam: We have a question on warm vs cold cache — if KV cache hits go from 45% to 70% how much tail improvement can we expect?
[08:50] Maya: Anecdotally p99 can drop by 30-50% in some cases because cache avoids expensive full autoregressive passes. We'll measure this directly in the replay.
[08:59] Carlos: For the POC timeline — what milestones should we commit to?
[09:03] Maya: Proposed 2-week POC: Week 0 (this week) gather traces & prompt set; Week 1 run harness iteratively, execute minimal matrix and produce preliminary report; Week 2, expanded runs and final report + recommendations. That assumes you provide traces within 3 business days.
[09:18] Priya: That timeline works if we can start on Monday.
[09:22] Jordan: We'll tentatively book time for the run-with-us session next Friday.
[09:26] [09:30] Speaker 1: quick aside — do you have any size limits for trace uploads?
[09:33] Maya: No strict limits — a few GB is fine, we prefer gzipped ndjson or csv with fields: request_id, timestamp, prompt_tokens, response_tokens, kv_hit, streaming_flag.
[09:45] Carlos: We'll export in that format.
[09:48] Priya: On the software side is there a recommended container spec?
[09:51] Maya: We provide a ready Dockerfile and a k8s job template for cluster runs. If you want to run on-prem we can provide Helm charts.
[09:59] Liam: Can we run minimal tests inside our VPC first? Security wants that.
[10:03] Jordan: Yes, Redwood Private option supports VPC peering and we can deploy the harness inside your VPC. For initial POC we usually test on hosted but we can do a VPC-run for the final validation.
[10:13] Dana: We'll need a data flow diagram for the auditors.
[10:17] Theo: I'll attach a diagram in the follow-up.
[10:20] [10:30] Maya: Now, a couple of gotchas — 1) streaming tests are very sensitive to network jitter because of chunked packets; if your client sits behind aggressive proxies that can inflate latencies. 2) batch windows: too large and UX suffers, too small and you lose batching gains. We'll test three window sizes.
[10:46] Carlos: Noted. Anything else on instrumentation?
[10:49] Maya: We'll tag trace rows with variant tags so we can compare across quantized vs baseline and streaming vs non-streaming.
[10:55] Priya: About failure modes — what does Redwood report for dropped connections?
[10:58] Maya: Harness logs include error type, retry counts, and end-to-end request timing. We'll calculate error budgets and surface retry storms.
[11:06] Carlos: Last thing — can we run a quick sanity sample now with a single prompt to verify harness connectivity?
[11:10] Maya: Sure, Jordan do you want to kick off the sample after the call? We can follow up in the Slack channel.
[11:15] Jordan: Yep I'll post the repo link and example payload in the shared channel as soon as we wrap.
[11:20] Priya: Great. I think we're aligned on deliverables.
[11:24] Jordan: Ok let's close with quick recap.
[11:26] Jordan: Recap: Redwood to share harness repo, config examples, and SOC2 docs. Nebula to provide traces and prompt set. Agreed test matrix (minimal 2hr run then extended 6-8hr matrix). Schedule run-with-us week of 2025-09-01. Action items in the doc.
[11:43] Carlos: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[11:46] Jordan: Thanks, talk soon.

End of transcript.
